articles.title: DPR Korea: Isolation deepens even as the country changes, says UN rights official

paras.en: DPR Korea: Isolation deepens even as the country changes, says UN rights official

The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) is building factories and hospitals, rolling out smartphones and mobile banking, and passing new laws at an unprecedented rate. But its people are more cut off from the outside world than at any point in the country’s history.

That is the picture painted by James Heenan, head of the UN human rights office (OHCHR) in the South Korean capital, Seoul. His team monitors the DPRK from beyond its borders because, as he puts it, “almost no one” can get in.

Speaking to UN News in New York, Mr. Heenan described a country where hunger remains a constant, forced labour touches every family and the border with China is so tightly sealed that even illegal crossings have all but stopped.
Yet he warned against seeing the DPRK – more commonly known as North Korea – as frozen in time. “The country is constantly changing, like every country in the world,” he said.
UN News: How does your office monitor human rights in the DPRK without direct access?

James Heenan: Well, it’s a tricky situation because we don’t have direct access to the country. Almost no one does at the moment. It’s very closed. In fact, historically, it’s never been more closed. We monitor, therefore, from outside.
We prioritise information from direct witnesses, so people who have suffered violations themselves, or who have witnessed them, or whose family members have suffered violations.

We also rely increasingly on Government information because the Government of the DPRK publishes more and more information, particularly over the past eight or nine years. We use other sources such as satellite imagery.
UN News: How many people have you interviewed?

James Heenan: Well, we’ve interviewed about a thousand people. That might not sound like much when you’re coming from some other parts of the world, but when you are dealing with what is possibly the most closed country in the world, that’s quite a lot.
UN News: How does the country’s isolation affect ordinary people?
James Heenan: There are very few people coming in or out of the country. There is very little information coming in or out of the country. That has a pretty serious impact on people.
They do not have access to the internet. They don’t know what’s going on outside or even inside the country.
The international humanitarian community, including the UN, has not had access for five or six years now, so when there’s a disaster, they don’t have access to that sort of support.
For average people, I think another impact is that there’s no access to certain types of medicines or treatment. There’s no access to certain types of food and so forth.
UN News: What is daily life like for an average family?
James Heenan: It depends very much on your status in society, your Songbun, as they call it, whether you are – essentially – in the loyal class, a wavering class or a hostile class.

For everyone, there’s a very high level of surveillance from the earliest years, both at home, in the workplace and at school. You have the risk of Government working groups arriving at the house at any time of the day or night to check electronic equipment to see whether there’s any forbidden information.
Food has always been a problem in the DPRK. Every single person we’ve spoken to has talked about hunger at some point.

We’ve had people tell us that one of the ways they realised things were different outside the country was when they escaped to China and saw that everyone was eating white rice. White rice is a luxury in the DPRK.
I think forced labour is also part of everyone’s life. You have mobilisations. They call them shock brigades, where people are essentially required to provide free labour for public works.
You might be sent away for days, weeks, months or even years to work on difficult projects for no pay. It’s classic forced labour, and it affects the whole country.
In many places, schoolchildren are sent to the fields, particularly during harvest, to work. Our information and analysis indicate that it’s a form of forced labour involving children.
UN News: Harvests have reportedly been good. Why is there still concern about food?
James Heenan: There was a drought earlier this year, but the harvests have been okay.

When you add to that an unreformed production and distribution system, you can very quickly end up in a situation that may not be famine but certainly involves widespread nutritional problems across society.
During COVID, we saw starvation. We saw people starving to death. Not as badly as in the 1990s, but it still happened.
UN News: The government has emphasised economic development. Is it bringing relief?

James Heenan: The flagship programmes include things like the 20-by-10 project, which is to construct factories in 20 counties every year for 10 years. You also see a large amount of hospital construction.
This is welcome. Anecdotal evidence suggests that it is creating more jobs for people, and jobs that pay. There have always been jobs, but traditionally they often paid nothing.
The challenge is that we don’t know exactly what impact this is having on people because we can’t get into the country to monitor it.
We are concerned because we know from the weight of historical evidence that many of these large infrastructure projects can involve forced labour during construction.
UN News: What is happening with digital technology?
James Heenan: Our latest report talked about thousands of 3G telephone masts across the country. There are more than 20 types of smartphones available in the DPRK.

But the issue is that it all exists within a restricted environment, meaning there is no access to the internet. It is clearly also being used to, if not increase surveillance, at least make surveillance more efficient. So, technology is a two-sided coin.
At the same time, we know that people are very happy to be able to use their phones for mobile banking, which is now widely used in the DPRK.
UN News: What is your single biggest concern right now?
James Heenan: I think I would have to say that there is a real concern about isolation and the restrictions of people’s ability to move freely.

People cannot move in and out of the country, even illegally, which was always something of a pressure valve that allowed people to go to China, for example, to earn money and come back. That’s not even possible anymore.

If I may add a second concern, it is the issue of separated families. We still have many families separated between DPRK and the Republic of Korea, and to some extent Japan as a result of enforced disappearances by the DPRK in the past.
Those families are getting older and older. Hundreds or thousands of family members have died over the years because this is a long-standing issue.
The survivors are elderly, and we’re pushing for progress among all those countries, if for no other reason than as a confidence-building measure that would allow these families to meet.
It’s something that happened up until 2018, and we’re pushing for it to happen again.
UN News: Is there anything else you want to emphasise?
James Heenan: I think the situation in the DPRK is one where people sometimes think it’s unchanging, but it’s not.
The country engages with the UN. It engages on human rights issues. In that way, the situation there should not be forgotten.
We can’t just talk about the Korean Peninsula in terms of peace and security. We also have to remember the human rights dimension, which is the focus of the United Nations.

articles.title: Samarkand: A ‘living museum’ on the Silk Road grapples with a tourism boom

paras.en: Samarkand: A ‘living museum’ on the Silk Road grapples with a tourism boom
As the sun sets over Samarkand’s majestic Registan, its last rays glint across the turquoise mosaics. Dusk settles on the ancient square where great trade routes have crossed for centuries.
Tourists linger at the stalls as the lights come on, lending the square an air of mystery.

The Registan is part of historic Samarkand, a UNESCO World Heritage site. But this is more than a city of monuments. People live here; schools, shops and workshops are open, and old neighbourhoods stand alongside new districts.
UN News visited ahead of World Cities Day to ask: how can civil leaders preserve its heritage while it keeps growing?
That question is at the heart of Samarkand’s “Silk Road” International University of Tourism and Cultural Heritage, which trains specialists in both fields from a campus in the city centre.

The university’s rector, Professor Muhsinjon Kholmukhamedov, told UN News that for centuries Samarkand was a crossroads not only for trade, but for ideas, crafts and cultures, flourishing in the eighth and ninth centuries and again in the Timurid era, when it became a centre of science, culture and the arts.
The university began working with the World Tourism Organization, now UN Tourism, in 2023 and renewed the partnership this year.
“We are the first partner university of this organization. We have established cooperation in several areas,” the rector said.
It is translating courses from the organization’s online academy for residents and preparing to open an INSTO tourism observatory – the first in Central Asia.

The observatory will track not only visitor numbers, but tourism’s impact on jobs, the urban environment and residents’ daily lives, as similar observatories already do from Barcelona and Vienna to Gifu in Japan and Nuevo León in Mexico.
Heritage preservation is another strand of its UN work, through a UNESCO Chair. One challenge, Mr. Kholmukhamedov said, is the legacy of restoration work in the 1990s.

“Unfortunately, gypsum, concrete and rebar were used then. We are now conducting research with experts and providing evidence-based recommendations on the use of modern composite materials that do not damage the historic fabric of the monuments,” he said.
Laser scanning lets researchers build three dimensional models of buildings and spot dangerous deformations in time. “If there is a critical tilt, we try to support the structure,” the rector said.
He calls Samarkand a living museum, where people go to work, meet friends and eat out beside monuments of global significance – a city that teaches its residents to value history.

Visitors feel that energy too. “Visiting Samarkand always reminds me of its special hospitality and energy. It is truly inspiring to see the city grow so vibrant and culturally rich,” UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan Sabine Machl told UN News.
Legend has it that Amir Timur picked his capital by having meat hung in several cities to see where it would take longest to spoil.
In Samarkand, the rector said, it stayed fresh longest – thanks, he believes, to the climate, the Zarafshan River and the nearby mountains.
Legend or not, Samarkand’s place in a fertile oasis at the crossroads of trade routes shaped its fortunes – and made it a welcome stop for merchants after arduous journeys.

Today, according to the rector, new railways are expected to connect Uzbekistan with China and Afghanistan, and on to South Asia, while a planned high speed highway should cut the Samarkand–Tashkent journey to about two and a half hours. Both are due for completion between 2030 and 2032.
The skies are busier too, with direct flights from Samarkand to more than 40 destinations.

According to Mr. Kholmukhamedov, about 1.2 million tourists visited Uzbekistan in 2016, compared with nearly 12 million in 2025. He estimates Samarkand alone received around seven million visitors last year; more than 10 million came in the first nine months of 2026, and the city expects around 14 million by year’s end.
Many come for the food – not least Samarkand palov - a rice pilaf – cooked and served in layers with local sesame oil. Uzbek palov culture is on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
Rapid growth is raising urgent questions about housing for Samarkand’s own residents – fitting, as this year’s World Cities Day theme is Urban Renewal: Affordable Housing for All.

More than 1,100 apartment buildings have gone up in Samarkand Region over the past eight years. UN-Habitat is now developing the Samarkand Housing Profile, Uzbekistan’s first, with the national Government.
Our generation’s task is to preserve Samarkand while making it future proof so that it stays liveable for future generations while keeping its identity, through resilient communities — Katja Schaefer

The city’s master plan to 2040 foresees a big expansion of housing, but also looks at the condition, energy efficiency, affordability and upkeep of existing homes – most of them individual houses. The Profile will recommend ways to make adequate housing more affordable, resilient and sustainable for all.
“In Samarkand, heritage is not only the monuments. It is also the mahallas, the traditional neighbourhoods where people live and where community life happens.

“The best approach is to upgrade homes and services in place rather than replace them: better water, heating and energy efficiency, sensitive renovation that respects the historic urban fabric, and new growth steered to areas outside the historic core,” Katja Schaefer, a UN-Habitat representative working on the project with local specialists, told UN News.
“Above all, residents should be involved in decisions about their neighbourhoods. Done this way, heritage and better living conditions support each other,” she said.

“Every era has left its mark,” she added. Much of the Soviet era housing and infrastructure is now outdated, and since independence the city has grown rapidly, at times without a plan, squeezing the green spaces that make it pleasant to live in.
Ms. Schaefer hopes the new master plan and the Green City Action Plan will tackle these challenges together.
In August, Samarkand and Tashkent joined the Green Cities Network of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), a group of cities working towards greener, healthier urban environments.

“What struck me most in Samarkand is how much of its greatness came from being a meeting place. Its position on the Silk Road made it a crossroads of trade and cultures for centuries, and it drew scholars from across the region.
“Under Ulugh Beg, it became one of the world’s leading centres of astronomy, mathematics and science. That spirit of exchange and innovation is still part of the city’s identity,” she said.

“Our generation’s task is to preserve Samarkand while making it future proof so that it stays liveable for future generations while keeping its identity, through resilient communities,” Ms. Schaefer said.

articles.title: Breaking the silence in Mexico’s barracks

paras.en: Breaking the silence in Mexico’s barracks

In Mexico’s armed forces, an order from a superior is meant to be obeyed without question. For many women in uniform, investigative journalist Zorayda Gallegos found, that can include an order to step into an officer’s bedroom.
“If an officer says, ‘Come into my bedroom,’ she must go in, otherwise she would be disobeying an order from her superior,” she told UN News.

Her investigation into sexual violence inside the military has won her the 2026 Breach/Valdez Award for Journalism and Human Rights. It has also made her a target, in one of the most dangerous countries in the world to be a reporter.
Her story, told ahead of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes Against Journalists on Monday, shows both why a free press matters and how much it can cost.
Her report, Sexual violence in the barracks: an X-ray of impunity, tracked more than 520 women who reported sexual offences over a 12-year period.
Only three per cent of those cases ended in a conviction. The other 97 per cent led to no effective sanctions.
This is not an isolated problem, Ms. Gallegos says, but a structural one. It reaches beyond the barracks into military schools and hospitals.
She also documented how high-ranking officials cover up abuse, and how gender inequality and institutional obstacles discourage victims from filing complaints at all.

For Ms. Gallegos, part of the problem starts with military training itself, which she describes as “a very hierarchical, top-down system where women are always taught to follow orders from their superiors”.
That leaves female soldiers vulnerable to the very officers they answer to.

Deep-rooted sexism makes things worse, she maintains, shaping who gets which jobs and who gets promoted. Female soldiers are often assigned tasks associated with “caregiving and nursing, even though they are qualified for higher-ranking positions,” she explains.
Women who do get their cases to court risk being victimised all over again. Some judicial rulings, she found, contain sexist remarks or lack any gender perspective.

Inside the institution, she says, the psychological support offered to complainants is geared towards getting them to forgive their aggressors, forget what happened and carry on with their military careers.
The men accused, meanwhile, are often given recommendations rather than punishments – “that’s the maximum”, Ms. Gallegos alleges.
To break the cycle of silence and impunity, she believes more women are needed in senior military leadership and decision-making roles, and in the judiciary and prosecution services.
Exposing all this has come at a personal cost. Ms. Gallegos has faced intimidating remarks, veiled threats and pressure because of her work.
She still defends the right to publish information in the public interest, and to report independently and impartially.

In Mexico, that takes courage. The UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) regularly highlights the country as one of the deadliest in the world for the press, even though it is not officially at war.

Collusion between organized crime and local authorities is a serious threat to reporters, and its effects are felt at every level of the justice system. Journalists investigating politics or crime face threats, kidnapping, enforced disappearance and murder, and many are forced to flee abroad.
According to UNESCO which tallies threats to media workers worldwide, 154 journalists have been murdered in Mexico in the past 20 years.
The agency has confirmed that eight journalists have been murdered in Mexico so far in 2026.
Press freedom groups including Article 19 and Reporters Without Borders (RSF) put the toll at nine, after the killing of Hamurabi Huesca Manzano in Oaxaca on 9 October.
The award Ms. Gallegos won carries the names of two of those killed. Miroslava Breach and Javier Valdez were assassinated because of their work.
“They always stood for brave journalism, rooted in their communities and committed to telling uncomfortable truths. Until it cost them their lives. That should never have happened,” she said.

articles.title: America's next great heavyweight? 'Stop looking. I'm already here!'

paras.en: Da’Mazion Vanhouter: America's next great heavyweight? 'They can stop looking. Because I’m already here!'

America is searching for its next great heavyweight - and Da’Mazion Vanhouter is determined to answer the call; "I'm here for it!" he says; Watch Vanhouter on the undercard of Chris Billam-Smith vs Cheavon Clarke on Saturday, live on Sky Sports
American boxing needs a great heavyweight champion, and Da’Mazion Vanhouter is here to audition for the role.
Vanhouter is in the early stage of his professional career but the prospect has been blasting through his recent opposition.
An explosive puncher, he's on a run of seven consecutive inside-the-distance victories. Overall nine of his 10 stoppage wins have come in the first round.
- Usyk considering cruiserweight return 'to make history again'
- Canelo returns to beat Mbilli and reclaim world title in Riyadh
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📺

His last fight caught the eye especially. Against the six foot eight inches tall Raphael Akpejiori in Las Vegas, it looked like Vanhouter's left shoulder was badly wrenched out of position. He responded immediately - viciously knocing Akpejiori out with his other hand.
"It was just in the moment a very sharp pain, how my shoulder was angled," he told Sky Sports. "It wasn't too crazy.
"I'm just here to fight and showcase my skills."

Vanhouter is still only 21 years old and 13 fights into a professional career that began when he was just 17. As a teenager remarkably he boxed down at super-welterweight. He's put on nearly 80lbs since then as he's developed into a heavyweight.
"I've grown into my frame but I still fight the same, the same movement, the same speed, I think I've gotten faster and obviously I hit harder now than I did before," Vanhouter said.

America was once the home of heavyweight boxing. Over the last decade, with the exception of Deontay Wilder, European fighters have dominated the heavyweight division. It's prompted a search to find America's next great heavyweight.
"They already stopped looking. Because I'm already here," he said with a beaming smile. "I'm here for it. That's the role I've taken, it's normal.
"I wouldn't be boxing if I didn't want to be the best. That means I want to be the best heavyweight."
High expectation can lead to a harsh fall. Moses Itauma, only 21 years old too, was, and is, the next great hope in British heavyweight boxing.
But even Itauma came unstuck in his first world title fight, losing surprisingly to Filip Hrgovic.
"You just can't rush the journey. It just wasn't his time and he just wasn't prepared for what happened," Vanhouter reflected.
The next step in Vanhouter's journey is a scheduled eight rounder against Ivan Balaz at the Copper Box Arena in London this Saturday, live on Sky Sports.
It's the American's fourth fight with Dana White's high-profile Zuffa Boxing promotion.
White believes that in Vanhouter they have a star for the future. "It would be great to have an unbelievable American heavyweight," White told Sky Sports.
"What America definitely needs is some heavyweights. Obviously we're high on him, we believe in him and that's exactly what we need for boxing in America."
Watch Vanhouter on the undercard of Chris Billam-Smith vs Cheavon Clarke on Saturday, live on Sky Sports.

articles.title: From crisis to champion: Antonelli's historic turnaround

paras.en: Kimi Antonelli: How F1's youngest ever world champion went from crisis point during his debut campaign to dominating the 2026 season

Kimi Antonelli finished third in the Mexico City GP on Sunday to become Formula 1's youngest ever world champion; the Italian's triumph was made all the more remarkable by the struggles he faced during his debut F1 campaign last year

When Mercedes announced in August 2024 that they were fast-tracking Kimi Antonelli - who had turned 18 just days earlier - into one of Formula 1's most desirable seats, expectations could not have been set much higher.
Fast-forward a little more than two years, and the Italian has delivered on his billing as a generational talent by becoming the sport's youngest world champion at the age of 20.
Even with expectations set so high, winning a title in just his second season in F1 has seen Antonelli surely exceed even the wildest dreams of Mercedes chief Toto Wolff.
But the most remarkable thing about Antonelli's triumph is the fact that this sporting fairy tale didn't initially go to plan, starting from the day before his signing was announced.
After Antonelli was crowned at the chequered flag of Sunday's Mexico City Grand Prix, Sky Sports F1 look back at his remarkable journey to this moment.
Shock Hamilton exit leads to Wolff gamble
Mercedes were left stunned in February 2024 when Lewis Hamilton announced that he had decided to leave the team he had won six of his seven championships with to join Ferrari the following year.

Once the dust had settled on the biggest driver transfer in the sport's history, Wolff's attention shifted to finding a new team-mate for George Russell, whose strong first two campaigns with the team had suggested he was a world champion in waiting.

The Austrian's top target appeared to be Red Bull's Max Verstappen, while the likes of Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz, who was making way for Hamilton at Ferrari, provided very solid and experienced options.
The wildcard for Wolff was Antonelli, who had been scouted by Mercedes as he dominated the European karting scene and signed by the team in 2019 as a 12-year-old.
Antonelli starred as he worked his way through the junior categories, so much so that Mercedes had him skip Formula 3 to go straight up to Formula 2 in 2024.

It's unclear whether Wolff had planned to loan Antonelli out to another team, as was the case when Russell, also a product of Mercedes' junior programme, spent his first three seasons in F1 at Williams, but the opening created by Hamilton's departure changed everything.

An unprecedented testing programme was arranged that allowed Antonelli big chunks of track time in Mercedes' cars from recent seasons. It was surely in those sessions, rather than a slightly underwhelming F2 campaign in which he finished sixth, that Wolff saw enough to convince him to roll the dice.

Some speculated that a factor in Wolff's decision was his regret at missing out on signing Verstappen as a teenager a decade earlier and wanting to ensure there was no way the sport's next generational talent would somehow end up in the clutches of a rival team.
Crisis point? Tears and 'underwhelming' Wolff

Antonelli was not only replacing the most successful driver in the sport's history in Hamilton, but the only real example of someone of his age being given a chance at a top team was when Red Bull promoted Verstappen from their junior squad during the 2017 season.
Even in that case, the Dutchman had 23 Grands Prix under his belt.
While it had become clear in the paddock that Antonelli had been chosen to partner Russell in 2025, Mercedes arranged a grand announcement around the 2024 Italian Grand Prix in Monza.

The plan was for him to make his first appearance in F1 practice on the Friday, before his signing was officially announced on Saturday. That is what happened, but only after Antonelli had destroyed the car by spinning into a barrier at high speed just 10 minutes into the session.

Six months later, Antonelli's first F1 qualifying session didn't go to plan either as he was knocked out of Q1 in Melbourne. But he would drive a mature race to fight back to fourth in the wet, and make a generally solid start to the season, with a Sprint pole position in Miami offering the first real glimpse of the speed that had been promised.
A first Grand Prix podium followed in Canada in June, but instead of pushing on from there, the Antonelli story reached its darkest moments.

There was the difficult sight of the teenage boy dabbing at his tearful eyes with a tissue as he attempted to conduct his media responsibilities in Belgium after an early qualifying exit, before Monza once more failed to provide any home comforts.

Having scored just one point across the five preceding races, Antonelli endured a torrid weekend at the Temple of Speed, which saw a crash in practice throw off his preparations before he finished ninth in the race. The Mercedes W16 car was far from best-in-field, but Russell had got it in the top five at five of those six races.
Wolff had been steadfast in his backing of Antonelli throughout the year, which meant it felt extremely significant when the Austrian was publicly critical of his young star for the first time.
"Underwhelming this weekend, underwhelming," Wolff said. "You can't put the car in the gravel bed and expect to be there. All of the race was underwhelming."
Wolff caveated his criticism by insisting he retained belief in his driver, but the comments raised doubts over whether Mercedes would persist with Antonelli if there wasn't an upturn in performance.

The tough love from Wolff appeared to work as Antonelli found some form to deliver a stronger final third of the year, with a memorable drive, once more in the wet, in Brazil providing a season's-best second-placed finish.
There was a major shift in the sport's landscape over the winter as the introduction of new chassis and power unit regulations effectively reset the playing field.

Having failed to contend for titles during the previous generation of rules from 2022 to 2025, Mercedes were installed as pre-season favourites, with paddock murmurings establishing a widespread belief that the Silver Arrows had aced their new engine - as they did in 2014 - and would start strongly.

While the change in competitive order of teams was anticipated, there was less of an expectation that alterations in driver performance could be similarly dramatic. For that reason, Russell was considered the clear favourite to claim the drivers' title.

While Russell lived up to expectations by taking pole position and winning the opening race of the season in Australia, perhaps more important in the long run was the second place Antonelli salvaged after an unnecessary crash in final practice threatened to leave him starting from the back of the grid.

Having avoided calamity, Antonelli took advantage of a little bit of luck as Russell suffered technical issues in Chinese Grand Prix qualifying to take pole, and backed that up by claiming the first race victory of his career a day later.

The result was the start of a streak that will live long in F1's history books, with Antonelli going on to reel off the first five victories of his career in successive races as wins followed in Japan, Miami, Canada and Monaco.
Russell was left dumbfounded. The title chance he had waited patiently for was suddenly being snatched away.

The Brit appeared in denial to begin with as he attributed the results to various external factors, but by the time Antonelli dominated and Russell finished 12th on a Monaco weekend where few expected Mercedes to win, it had become clear to all that the generational talent had well and truly arrived.

Wolff recently reflected: "It's been 30 or more years that I've tried to understand racing drivers' brains, and I still don't know what has happened (to Antonelli) over the winter. His ability to process and deliver something that's outstanding, which we didn't see coming."
Monza magic and Austin excellence close the show

However, winning a title rarely comes without adversity, and it struck during the European summer as an engine failure took Antonelli out of a podium finish in Barcelona, before a wheel-guard failure denied him a potential victory at the British Grand Prix a few weeks later.

Russell was back within 25 points, while Hamilton was also in striking distance a further seven points adrift, and Mercedes were no longer as dominant as they had been in the early stages of the season.
With the pressure on, Antonelli responded by winning the next race in Belgium and then delivering podiums either side of the summer break to rebuild his lead, but the best was still to come.
Unlike a year earlier when Oscar Piastri had appeared on course for his maiden title before suffering a dramatic loss of form and finishing third in the standings, Antonelli seemed to get better.

Given what had happened to Antonelli on his previous two appearances at Monza, it seemed there was a psychological element to a decision being made for him to take an engine penalty at the race, which would drop him to 19th on the grid, perhaps relieving the pressure that had hindered him at home in the past.

It turned out to be a masterstroke, as Antonelli scythed his way through the field to win with ease, producing a performance that belongs with legendary displays of the past: Verstappen in Brazil in 2024, Hamilton in Germany in 2018, Michael Schumacher in Belgium in 1995.
The drive alone was enough to make it the standout moment of this season, but there were two further elements that made it even more significant.
The result demoralised Russell, who had started from second on the grid, and made it a question of when, not if, Antonelli was going to close out his triumph.

And then there was the turning of the tifosi, Ferrari's fiercely loyal legion of fans in red, many of whom found themselves cheering for Antonelli and proudly singing the Italian national anthem as the boy wonder stood on the top step of the podium.

While it was less eye-catching than the Monza display, Antonelli would also produce a different type of brilliant victory at the United States Grand Prix as he overcame Mercedes' struggles with their new upgrade package to deny an in-form Verstappen pole, before producing an unexpectedly dominant race to win comfortably.

Antonelli could hardly be more popular within his Mercedes team, but the result was a massive moment for the Silver Arrows as it confirmed there is potential in the development path they've been pursuing ahead of a 2027 season where Red Bull and Verstappen look primed to return to title contention.

Wolff described it as Antonelli's "best race" in F1, before being reminded of what had happened in Monza seven weeks earlier. The Austrian admitted he may have been slightly forgetful, but insisted the performances belonged in the same bracket.

The mathematical equation after the Austin victory turned the Mexico City Grand Prix into something of a title parade for Antonelli, but he still overcame illness and nerves to produce a strong performance that earned him a podium finish in third.

While there was no crowning victory, the fairy-tale scene on the podium was near perfect as race winner Verstappen and second-placed Hamilton - the two most successful drivers on the current grid - hoisted Antonelli onto their shoulders, creating an iconic image that will live long in the memory.
The problem for the rest of the grid, and his team-mate Russell in particular, is that Antonelli should theoretically get better and better.

As Wolff explained in Austin, "the work of nine years" and more than £10m has gone into developing Antonelli. There is little doubt that both the team and driver himself will continue to leave no stone unturned in maximising his extraordinary talent.

Perhaps crucial to that process has been Mercedes allowing Antonelli to act his age in some ways, with videos of him pranking his engineers and vice versa shared on the team's social media channels throughout the season.

While Mercedes have created a familial environment for Antonelli to thrive in, credit must also go to his own parents, who have raised a young man who has achieved the remarkable feat, at least to this point of his career, of being almost universally popular.

His father Marco, a former racing driver himself, has been an ever-present in the paddock, but has also taken enough of a step back to allow an extremely close father-son relationship to flourish without creating too many challenges for the team.
You'd be hard pushed to find anyone in the paddock - driver, team boss or journalist - who would have a bad word to say about Antonelli, who does just about everything with a smile on his face.
Even McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, whose squad were constructors' champions in 2024 and 2025, spoke of his pride and excitement as an Italian at seeing what Antonelli is doing.
Away from the paddock, Antonelli's age and charm have made him extremely popular with younger fans of the sport, and he will surely continue to bring new followers in Italy and beyond.

With Italy's passionate fans desperate for a new hero amid their men's football team's continued slump and tennis star Jannik Sinner struggling with injuries, Antonelli is quite possibly about to become the nation's most popular sporting figure.

If F1 bosses had any fears over the sport lacking some star power when Hamilton eventually retires, the emergence of Antonelli will have them sleeping easier, with global superstardom an inevitably if he continues on this path.
The other question that probably won't go away until it happens, whether that's in five, 10 or 15 years, is whether Antonelli will follow in Hamilton's footsteps by moving from Mercedes to Ferrari.
Formula 1 next heads to Brazil for the final leg of the triple header with the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from November 6-8, live on Sky Sports F1. Stream Sky Sports with NOW.

articles.title: Haskell backs Borthwick, Pollock as England prepare for Nations Championship

paras.en: England Rugby: Steve Borthwick and Henry Pollock backed by James Haskell ahead of Nations Championship fixtures

James Haskell believes Steve Borthwick is the right man to lead England at the 2027 Rugby World Cup and shares his excitement over rising star Henry Pollock ahead of November's Nations Championship fixtures against Australia, Japan and New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham
James Haskell has backed Steve Borthwick as "the right man for the job" as England prepare for the conclusion of the inaugural Nations Championship in November.

Borthwick oversaw England's worst-ever Six Nations campaign earlier this year, with four losses from their five matches, but despite growing pressure the RFU have publicly expressed their support for Borthwick through to the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia.
This month, England will face Australia, Japan and New Zealand ahead of Finals Weekend, which takes place November 27-28 at Twickenham.
Former England international Haskell, who earned 77 Test caps between 2007 and 2019, insists it is not the time to change the head coach.
"The RFU have got behind Steve Borthwick, and rightly so," Haskell told Sky Sports.
"I think he's the right man for the job."
Borthwick oversaw a 12-game unbeaten streak ahead of the 2026 Six Nations, and Haskell insists the change in performance is not as stark as the critics might suggest.
"It's never as bad as you think it is and it's never as good as you think it is," he said.
"I think there's a lot of talent, and without being a super nerd - which rugby pundits often can be - if you look at the stats, we create lots of opportunities.
"When we were on our unbeaten run of 12 games, 83 per cent of the time we got into the 22-metre line, we took away points.
"When we were losing games, we were making the same opportunities but coming away with points less than 33 per cent of the time.
Haskell also praised the ego and style of rising star Henry Pollock.

The Northampton Saints back-row who made headlines by becoming the first rugby union player to sign for Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency back in March, could be given more international chances in the coming weeks.
"He's definitely got that X-factor, in terms of the way he plays," said Haskell.
"He's probably the most talked about rugby player at the moment. He creates opinion and challenges opinion - and that's what makes the world go round now.
"But when he gets opportunities on the field, he delivers… I'm very excited that he will hopefully get more of a chance to play for England.
"It will challenge some of the stuffier, more stoic sides of the upper echelons, and of the fanbase, who like their sports stars manageable and with a bit of ego, but not too much.
"If someone could bring that cohesion together, keep raising awareness and building superstars like Henry Pollock, you're going to be in a great place."

articles.title: U.S. set to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, despite risk they’ll be returned to Taliban
articles.author: Jennifer Jett

paras.en: The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan on the first flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.
The proposed deportation flight, which has not been publicly announced, could take place as early as Monday, according to rights advocates and families of detainees.

Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban, which is now back in power. The deportees could face severe repercussions should Pakistan return them to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan as is widely expected.

Afghans driven from their country by war and political instability have been welcomed by the U.S. for decades, including tens of thousands who fled the country following the chaotic withdrawal of U.S.-led forces in 2021. President Donald Trump halted admissions for Afghans and other refugees when he returned to office last year as part of a broader immigration crackdown.

His administration has deported thousands of people to countries that are not their own, many of them in Africa, in what immigration lawyers say is an effort to skirt international laws against returning asylum-seekers to the countries they fled from. The legality of these so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.

It is not clear what kind of formal agreement the U.S. may have with Pakistan, but the senior administration official said the U.S. charter flight would not be able to land there without the Pakistan government’s knowledge and approval. The deportation plan was earlier reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times.
Bloomberg cited a federal government official familiar with the plans as a source for its report, while The New York Times cited three U.S. officials.

Shawn VanDiver, president of the San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said it had confirmed that in recent days, at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, 19 of them without legal representation.
He said it was possible that there were hundreds of Afghans at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, which has served as a hub for ICE detainees before their deportation from the U.S.

If the U.S. sends Afghan detainees to Pakistan, they are not likely to be there long. Pakistan, which has hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a sweeping crackdown in 2023, pressuring hundreds of thousands of Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deporting others.

They are arriving to an Afghanistan battered by multiple humanitarian crises, including widespread malnutrition, as well as an ongoing military conflict with neighboring Pakistan and a dramatic rollback of women’s rights under the Taliban’s hard-line Islamic policies.
VanDiver said the Trump administration would most likely be aware that Afghans sent to Pakistan would be at high risk of being returned to Afghanistan.
“You don’t have to be that smart to figure out that they’re sending them to Pakistan so that Pakistan will finish the job,” he said.

Regardless of whether they worked with the U.S. military, VanDiver said, any Afghans flown from the U.S. would be viewed with suspicion by the Taliban and at risk of persecution, imprisonment or worse.
That does not appear to be a major concern for the White House, said the senior administration official, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
“The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.

VanDiver and others say the Trump administration’s treatment of Afghan allies could also have long-term consequences for U.S. national security by discouraging people in other countries from working with U.S. forces in future conflicts.
Asked whether the Trump administration was concerned about that, the official said, “I don’t think they care.”

The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.” ICE did not respond to a request for comment.
A State Department spokesperson said the agency had “no plans to announce.”

“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens,” the spokesperson said.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

The senior administration official said the Afghans on the flight could include people with deportation orders, people who were turned down for asylum and people whose temporary protected status was terminated by the Trump administration. Many of the Afghans facing deportation requested asylum after crossing into the U.S. from Mexico, VanDiver said, and some of their cases are still pending.

Charlotte, a U.S. citizen whose Afghan husband has been in ICE detention since early 2025, said he had been moved to the Louisiana facility from Pennsylvania this month and told he would be deported in early November. She declined to be identified by her full name out of concern that her husband could be targeted by the Taliban.

Charlotte said she and her husband, whose asylum case has been pending for nine years, were visiting family in Maryland last year when he accidentally crossed into West Virginia and was pulled over. Though he was carrying his valid Illinois driver’s license, he did not have his work permit with him.

“When he was pulled over,” she said, “the sheriff actually said, ‘I’m an ICE agent. You’re going to immigration custody. I don’t care if the charges are dismissed, or I don’t care if you have a five-year work permit or Social Security card. I don’t care if you’re legal. Trump’s administration just took over — you’re going directly to immigration custody.’”

Charlotte sold their home in Illinois and moved to Maryland with their son, now 6, in order to be able to visit her husband at the ICE facility where he was held in Pennsylvania, about 100 miles away.
“I lost my nice house, our car, we left everything behind,” she said.
Over the next 20 months, when she took her son to see his father at the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, they were always separated by plexiglass.
“They never let him hug him one time,” Charlotte said. “We just sat there and cried every time.”
But at least they knew where he was and that he was OK, she said. Now that he’s in Louisiana, she said, “we can’t even visit or even say goodbye, he’s over 1,200 miles away.”

With her husband potentially being sent to Pakistan or Afghanistan — a country he hasn’t been to since 2016 — the uncertainty is even greater; Charlotte said he is growing his beard to comply with the Taliban’s strict rules for men’s facial hair.
“I’m just terrified that he’s not going to be safe,” she said, “or he’s going to be held in the jail and there’s nothing I can do.”
Charlotte said she believed her husband had been targeted for deportation because of a past conviction for a nonviolent crime that has since been resolved.
“I still don’t think this should end our entire life, for a child not to see his dad,” she said.
“He’s completely devastated and traumatized,” she said of their son. “He wants to fight. He wants to go protest. He wants to speak to Donald Trump. He basically knows so much more than he should.”

The preparations for the deportation flight come nearly a year after a shooting in Washington that killed one National Guard member and seriously injured another. The suspect, an Afghan national who served alongside U.S. troops in Afghanistan and was evacuated to the U.S. in 2021, had been granted asylum by the Trump administration. Immigration restrictions were tightened after the shooting.

VanDiver said the Trump administration may also be using the Pakistan flight as a test case for Camp As Sayliyah, a U.S.-run camp in Qatar where more than 1,000 Afghans who had been slated for resettlement in the U.S. have been stranded since Trump returned to office last year.

Asked about VanDiver’s claim, the White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson again said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.”

According to AfghanEvac, the camp was housing 287 men, 319 women and 433 children as of July. Most of them have been approved for U.S. resettlement after extensive vetting, and many of the adults worked alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan.
The group at Camp As Sayliyah also includes 150 relatives of U.S. military service members, AfghanEvac said.
Afghan refugees in Qatar protest over travel suspension

The State Department said earlier this year that everyone would be removed from the camp by March 31, a deadline that was later extended to Sept. 30. In September, the Trump administration delayed its closure by another nine months, The Associated Press reported.
Earlier this year, the administration considered sending the Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is experiencing the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

In a statement on Friday, AfghanEvac accused the Trump administration of planning the Afghan deportation flight as the country is distracted by next week’s midterm election, “hoping no one is watching.”
“The government won’t say where these flights land, because it knows what happens to the people on them when they do,” the group said. “A government confident in what it is doing does not hide it.”

articles.title: Parents fight move to close 120-year-old Catholic primary school
articles.author: Grace Crivellaro

paras.en: The Bishop of Wollongong announced last week that Catholic primary school St Michael's Mittagong will amalgamate with another Catholic school in Bowral.
More than 1,600 people have signed a petition opposing the amalgamation.
The closure is scheduled for 2029. The Diocese of Wollongong says it will begin a "detailed exploratory process" for the future use of the site.
More than 1,600 people are opposing the closure of a 120-year-old Catholic primary school after parents say they were blindsided by the decision.

The Bishop of Wollongong Brian Mascord announced last Thursday St Michael's school in Mittagong would close in 2029, with all students assured a place at the site of St Thomas Aquinas Catholic Parish Primary School in Bowral.

In a letter to 190 families, the bishop labelled the move as an amalgamation and "bringing together" of the schools, under the new name Corpus Christi Catholic Parish Primary School, Mittagong-Bowral.
Michelle Hinton is one of the parents "blindsided" by the move and said the school's faith-based education is deeply important to her.
"I opened up the letter and just burst into tears,"
"Some of the parents have used the word flabbergasted, some have used the words betrayed."
In the letter, the bishop acknowledged the decision would come as a shock.
"This is understandable and a testament to the great experience you and your family have had at St Michael's or St Thomas Aquinas," Bishop Mascord said.
"At the same time, as Bishop, it is my responsibility to carefully consider and respond as best I can to the various needs of all people living in parishes within the diocese."
He said the call was made in response to a proposal from the Mittagong-Bowral parish.
"While no decision has been made about how the site at Mittagong may be used from 2029, this change means the parish can explore options to meet broader community needs," he wrote.

The Diocese of Wollongong said in a statement on Monday that it was left with no other option but to amalgamate the schools after it assessed "enrolment trends, demographic data and the parish's assessment of long-term financial viability".
Ms Hinton said some parents would not be able to uproot their children, and that others would face a slightly longer commute if they choose to attend the amalgamated school.
She said she was deeply concerned about the erasure of a historically significant site for many Southern Highlands residents, adding that parents were not consulted about the fate of the school.

"The grief goes beyond bricks and mortar, it's the history of the school, the connection with St Michael, all the little stories held within those gates that could be erased by the lack of community consultation," she said.
"I would like to see them acknowledge the upset and upheaval of this decision.
"I'd like them to review what they've done; I'd like to see Bishop Brian support the parish, and I'd like to see the archbishop review this decision."
Former student Kathryn Dovey launched a petition to fight the decision and save the school, which has garnered more than 1,600 signatures in three days.
"I went to this school 30 years ago and it became such an important part of my life that I decided to send my own children there," she said.
"My eldest son is in kindergarten and I have two other children that would be due to start in 2028 and 2031."
Ms Dovey said she had heard enrolments had been declining at both schools, but that St Michael's appeared to be a "thriving school".
"We've been told that this is an opportunity to meet community needs to close Mittagong … but we haven't been told what those needs are," she said.
The diocese said it was committed to preserving the histories of each school.
It said staff retention will be a "strong focus" in the amalgamated school and that there will be no reduction in enrolment capacity.
Secretary of the Independent Education Union Carol Matthews said St Michael's teachers were concerned by the decision.
"The teachers at Mittagong are concerned, they're sad, they really value their community school," she said.

The announcement comes after several Catholic schools in Sydney's northern beaches were told they would have to share a principal, with the Newcastle-Maitland diocese separately making over 50 school librarian jobs redundant.

articles.title: Could government spending cuts help fight inflation? Here are the facts
articles.author: Tom Crowley

paras.en: The Reserve Bank is tipped to increase interest rates tomorrow because of an ongoing concern that inflation is not under control. It would be the fifth hike of the year, and the 18th in five years.
The consequences are familiar: rates are a "blunt instrument", painful for all borrowers.

But is there an alternative? In the past week, much commentary has focused on whether government spending cuts could be a "precise instrument", taking pressure off inflation in a targeted way and alleviating the pain of high rates.
The government has flagged at least some fresh savings. So where could cuts come from, and could they influence inflation?
In simple terms, inflation happens when an economy is operating above capacity. When the demand to spend is more than what an economy can supply, the extra demand pushes prices up.

The cause can come from anywhere. The Reserve Bank thinks the resurgence of inflation in the past year has been driven by the Middle East war, an AI investment boom, and the fact Australia was already above capacity before those things.
Whatever its origins, economists worry about inflation becoming entrenched in an economy. RBA governor Michele Bullock explains it this way:
"High inflation hurts all Australians, especially the most vulnerable. Every household has seen how the price of everything has gone up in recent years. Pay packets don't go as far as they used to …
"It's critical that we stop [this] from becoming embedded in price-setting decisions across the economy or the problem will only become worse."
Policies to fight inflation can seek either to expand supply or suppress demand. While supply policies are important, demand suppression works quicker, and so is the main frontline response.

The aim is not to address the causes of inflation or to lower specific prices. For example, policymakers can do little about high fuel prices. Instead, they aim to take pressure off elsewhere as a counterweight.

The Reserve Bank has one main lever: higher interest rates. High rates suppress demand in multiple ways. Existing borrowers — people and businesses — pay more on their loans, leaving less money to spend elsewhere. New borrowing is discouraged.
Saving is encouraged, because the returns are higher. And Australian dollars become more expensive, pushing down overseas demand for our exports.
How government spending can help or hinder
The government's main lever is its budget. Every year, the government raises and spends hundreds of billions of dollars. Taxing more or spending less can directly reduce demand.
This can be a precise instrument because the government can choose exactly what programs it cuts, or exactly where it raises taxes.

In theory, it means the government can fight inflation with regard for "fairness" in a way that the Reserve Bank cannot, because it can decide who should bear the brunt of the pain. But inflicting pain with higher taxes or spending cuts is politically fraught.

And in fact, governments are often pulled in the other direction. When prices are high, voters expect relief in the form of tax cuts or subsidies. Governments often oblige, even though this can push up inflation by expanding demand rather than suppressing it.

The Albanese government has made a virtue of offering this sort of cost-of-living relief, and despite its criticisms, the Coalition has advocated for relief too. Treasurer Jim Chalmers argues this is justified, because the government has multiple roles:

"We have to balance the inflationary pressures in our economy with the fiscal pressures in our budget and try to do the best that we can for people… We think we've struck [the balance] relatively effectively."
How much has the Albanese government spent?

There are several ways to assess how the government has struck that balance. One is to look at the overall level of spending. On that measure, spending under the Albanese government is abnormally high, remaining at levels comparable to the pandemic.

But many of the drivers of this spending are long-term factors that are hard to control. Of the fastest-growing spending categories, only child care has been substantially expanded by the Albanese government. Another, the NDIS, has been curbed.

Another way to approach the question is to look at how the budget has changed under Labor. Taking the combined effect of all of the government's budget updates, the budget balance has improved in most years, meaning lower deficits and even two surpluses.
But that graph includes factors that the government cannot take responsibility for. In fact, even inflation itself has helped: inflation means people pay more income tax, improving the budget.
Stripping out these external factors shows a different picture, with the budget balance worse off in each year thanks to government decisions.

This is often described as the "truest" picture of the government's responsibility. But even this is imperfect, because the government argues that many of these "decisions" are unavoidable and would be made by all governments, like the indexation of some payments and the listing of new PBS medicines.
Each of these measures tells us something about the contribution of the government to inflation, but not everything. Doing that requires evaluating each government decision line by line.

Here are just a handful of the largest decisions highlighted in budget papers. This non-exhaustive list shows one of the reasons government ministers have defended their spending decisions. The items are central to the government's political narrative, including its changes to bulk-billing, cheaper child care and tax cuts.

In theory, the government could have taken pressure off inflation if it had decided against any of these new spending policies. But as well as any political consequences, the result would also be less money for the recipients of these policies.

Some of the government's political opponents have pointed to individual policies that could be cut. For example, the Coalition has named the Cheaper Home Batteries Program and the EV discount, among others. Independent MP Allegra Spender has named fuel tax credits, an existing subsidy that costs more than $10 billion a year.

Cutting some of these spending programs could mean fewer rate hikes — economist Chris Richardson estimates that $7 billion to $10 billion of spending cuts per year is equivalent to one rate hike (note: the figures in the table are over four years, not per year).

But the challenge for the government, and for other political parties, is deciding whether the pain of those spending cuts is preferable to the pain on borrowers from a rate hike. Either way, the intent is the same: to suppress demand.

articles.title: 'Impossible to get ahead': Canberra inflation rate rises above national average
articles.author: Madeleine Rojahn

paras.en: Household inflation has risen to 4.7 per cent in the ACT, with the national average being 4.3 per cent.
Canberrans are continuing to curb their spending, with small businesses seeing declining foot traffic.
An economics lecturer says inflation is not expected to come down anytime soon, with another rate increase on the horizon.
The ACT's inflation rate jumped to 4.7 per cent in the 12 months to September this year, and now sits above the national average of 4.3 per cent.
And with the RBA expected to lift the cash rate again tomorrow to 4.85 per cent — the highest rate since the 2008 global financial crisis — many households are doing all they can to curb their costs.
But for some Canberra business owners that means sales are down, with no end in sight.
"Nobody's out and about eating and obviously that hurts us," Casey Johnston, who runs a burrito business in Tuggeranong with her partner, said.
Ms Johnston said she was used to business "fluctuating" in the hospitality sector, but sales were "a lot lower" than past years.
"I feel like our foot traffic, people walking along the street just to find somewhere to eat for dinner or lunch, is definitely declining," Ms Johnston said.
"People bring people in [with] small business, and when there is no people, people are not stopping by."
Ms Johnston said they were also absorbing rising business costs including products and rent, rather than passing those costs onto customers.
"[It] is a hard battle because we can't increase our prices for our consumers, but we're definitely taking the hit of our products being more expensive ourselves," she said.
"We can't always afford wages and that kind of thing.
"If people aren't here then the employment is not necessarily needed all the time, and that can make things really tricky."
Senior lecturer in economics at the University of Canberra Dr John Hawkins said global oil prices were the main driver for rising inflation rates.
In the ACT specifically, the biggest drivers were fuel, electricity, childcare and school fees, new housing builds, and furniture, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
"You get these variations that are quite random," Dr Hawkins said.
"Our inflation's lower than Hobart, Darwin, and Adelaide, but it's a bit higher than Sydney and Melbourne."
Dr Hawkins also warned the Reserve Bank of Australia was likely to once again hike up interest rates.

"There's an 80 per cent chance that [homeowners] will probably be paying 0.25 per cent more on their mortgages from tomorrow, and the financial markets think if the Reserve Bank doesn't move tomorrow, they'll probably move in either December or early next year," he said.
"Raising interest rates will lower inflation because it will slow down the economy.
"By raising interest rates, it'll make saving more attractive, so people will spend less and save more."
Elanor, a hairdresser, said she has personally already cut down "literally everything" when it comes to discretionary spending.
"So no coffees out, no more expenditures," she said.

"Holidaying, going away, just being able to eat out — so not going out to restaurants, even though we've got all these beautiful restaurants and everything around us — no, I don't spend on that anymore."
Elanor said her workplace's clientele base had largely remained the same, but people were booking hair appointments less frequently than they normally would.
"It is impossible to get ahead at the moment, especially here in Canberra," she said.
"The cost of living is just skyrocketing."

articles.title: Young men and right-leaning podcasters helped Trump win in 2024. Both have soured on him
articles.author: Angela Hennessy

paras.en: Young men and right-leaning podcasters helped Trump win in 2024. Both have soured on him
'I feel like we got duped,' says one young Trump voter
Like many young men, Nicholas Aparicio's concerns about future employment, buying a home or even putting gas in his car are mounting.
"The idea of starting a family feels very out of reach these days," the 20-year-old told CBC News.
Aparicio, a political science student in Binghamton, N.Y., says he voted for Donald Trump in 2024 because he believed the president would improve the economy and his own prospects.

"The fact that he was so personable and he was this entertainer, it felt good to have him in your corner. Like, that's my guy. He's not like us, because he's a billionaire, but he's willing to empathize with us," Aparicio said. "He's going to fight for us."
Aparicio's attitude now: "I feel like we got duped."
While Aparicio is the president of the College of Republicans Binghamton Chapter, he's so disillusioned with the party that he’s not sure he will even vote in next week’s midterms.

Nick Aparicio, a political science student living in Binghamton, N.Y., voted for Donald Trump in 2024 because he believed the president would improve the economy and his own prospects. Aparicio thinks differently now. (Yanjun Li/CBC)

For years, it felt like many young men were all in on President Trump and his Make America Great Again platform. So were many popular right-leaning or "manosphere" podcasters, like Joe Rogan and Tucker Carlson, who helped spread Trump’s message in the run-up to the 2024 election.
Together, these groups helped get him re-elected.
But young men are increasingly turned off by Trump, and those podcasters are distancing themselves, too — a trend that experts say could swing House and potential Senate seats in the midterms.
"At this point, Democrats have a 26-point lead on Republicans amongst younger people," said John Della Volpe, director of polling at the Harvard Institute.
Midterms outcome rests largely on young men
Della Volpe’s recent poll found just nine per cent of young Americans believe the country is on the right track, while 69 per cent say they're fearful about the future.
The same poll found only 31 per cent of young men said they would definitely vote.
"Young men absolutely helped Trump win in the last election and if they don’t come out and vote in these midterms, it will change the outcome."
David Sasaki, a director at the American Institute for Boys and Men, says that many Gen Z men are avid listeners of podcasters like Rogan, Steven Bartlett and standup comedian Andrew Schulz.

"I think that [young men] feel that they are being spoken to, not just about. It's using language that they use, it's using cultural references and jokes they understand, it’s very relatable," Sasaki said.
Cross Country Checkup is asking: How will the U.S. midterm elections affect you? What questions do you have? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show.
He said that "authenticity, or at least perceived authenticity, is the currency of politics these days." He also said that podcasters fill a void in some young men.

"A lot of [them] are not growing up with mentors, role models or male adults in their real life, and they’re finding them online," Sasaki said. "They have a lot of influence over these voters, who matter a lot come election day."
Aparicio says while he doesn’t listen to one particular podcaster, like many of his peers, he consumes their content through social media clips.

In 2024, Rogan, Schulz and Theo Von all hosted Donald Trump on their shows and spoke about MAGA politics — which is, generally speaking, anti-establishment, anti-immigrant and anti-foreign entanglements — in a way that seemed to endorse it.

Last year, Schulz said on his podcast Flagrant that he regretted voting for Trump. In April, Carlson, the former Fox News personality and now host of the podcast The Tucker Carlson Show, also expressed regret at endorsing Trump in 2024, saying "I’m sorry for misleading people" and that he will be "tormented" by it.
Meanwhile, Rogan — still the most popular podcaster in the U.S. — has publicly criticized Trump twice: over the White House hosting a UFC fight this summer and the war in Iran.

Comedian and podcaster Theo Von, in glasses, arrives prior to the second inauguration of President Donald Trump at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 20, 2025. Since then, Von has been more critical of the president. (Al Drago-Pool/Getty Images)
CBC reached out to Rogan, Von, Schulz and Carlson for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.
Right-leaning podcasters mentioning Trump less

In an effort to quantify conservative podcasters' disenchantment with Trump, The Wall Street Journal studied how often podcasters such as Rogan and Ben Shapiro have referred to him since the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election. According to the Journal’s reporting, mentions of Trump have dropped 70 per cent.

"There were two main plunges: one was right after the election, after which it steadily dropped, and then it dipped again after the Iran war started," Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Mehta told CBC News.
Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Mehta has studied how right-leaning podcasters have covered Donald Trump since he was elected president a second time. (CBC)
"Podcasters and content creators are the predominant source of news for young people. But they also prioritize being seen as real and authentic — that’s the sell," Mehta said.
For Sasaki, a number of pivotal moments demonstrate the podcasters' shift away from Trump.
In early October, Theo Von, who hosts This Past Weekend, interviewed New York's left-leaning Mayor Zohran Mamdani. They discussed socialism, affordability and inequality.

"This to me showed what we already could see … that the conversation was really changing," said Sasaki. "In the lead-up to the 2024 election, [Von] had Trump on, who appeared very relatable. And then Mamdani went on the show and appeared even more relatable."
Sasaki also pointed to CBS News exit polling data that showed roughly 60,000 Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 also voted for Mamdani in 2025.

"What Trump and that campaign was able to do in 2024 was go to the spaces where young men were, speak to them in their vernacular with cultural references that they relate to, and say, ‘I know that you’re struggling, I see your struggles and we’re going to do something about it,’" Sasaki said.
But "assuming this demographic of young men is all in on MAGA and can’t swing [away] would be an error in judgment."
Trump out of step with young men: expert
Aparicio said that by potentially not voting in this year's midterms, "I want to emphasize the point that young men should not be taken for granted by the Republicans."
Podcaster Joe Rogan has publicly criticized Donald Trump twice this year, including calling the war in Iran a 'giant quagmire' and not what his MAGA followers voted for. (The Joe Rogan Show/YouTube)
Ultimately, Sasaki believes Trump may be missing what young men in 2026 really care about.
"This demographic is more worried than ever about the economy. They feel very little job security, many can’t imagine ever buying a home and are even living below the poverty line," he said.
Aparicio says Trump began looking untrustworthy shortly after he won in 2024.
"The first real sign was him campaigning that he would release the Epstein files and then began gaslighting his followers [when he took office] and saying they don't exist," he said.
He also believes the economy has gotten worse and that the U.S. involvement in the war in Iran and its endorsement of Israel's actions in Gaza are making things harder for Americans.
"Hopefully if I work hard, I will be able to afford a home and raise a family," Aparicio said.
"The way things are going, I really don’t feel sure about that."
With files from Eli Glasner and Lillie-Anne Cousee

articles.title: 'Despicable betrayal': Democrats stunned after Michigan congresswoman endorses Republican for Senate

paras.en: 'Despicable betrayal': Democrats stunned after Michigan congresswoman endorses Republican for Senate
Haley Stevens backs Mike Rogers after she lost party primary to Abdul El-Sayed

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers after Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.

Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he's focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
"At the end of the day I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding later: "None of this matters."
People in Grand Rapids, Mich., watch a televised debate between El-Sayed and Stevens on July 7. (Kristen Norman/The Associated Press)

Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is in a tight race with Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring.
Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party's effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump's second term.

Democrats had hoped Sunday would offer a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.

Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.

After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and fiancé Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, "I'm not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote."
Rogers, standing beside her, said he was "honoured" by her support.
Their appearance stunned Democrats, coming days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for her party's nominee.
The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement "shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about."
"We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Hertel wrote, and won't let such 11th-hour "distractions" deter the campaign.
Hertel later wrote that Stevens "is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."
Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers.
"This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens," Schumer wrote in a social media post.

Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.

Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats in the final days before Tuesday's vote, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.
"I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in a telephone interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers.
"This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank."
A voter arrives to cast their ballot during early voting for the midterm elections in Pontiac, Mich., on Saturday. (Brian Snyder/Reuters)

Dingell and other Democrats insist the party is united behind El-Sayed. Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions resurfaced, complicating efforts to deliver a unified closing message in crucial areas such as Detroit, where turnout could prove decisive.
As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan. A total of 4.5 million ballots were cast in the 2022 midterm election, a record for a nonpresidential year.

Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighbouring Oakland County, in the primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.

The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee's affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offence to an outside group's ad accusing him of disrespecting women.
Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his summer win.

Last week Stevens' fiancé told the Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to "shut out the hate and call it out."

But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.
"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," Stevens wrote. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."
El-Sayed responded: "So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let's all focus on the task at hand."
He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said, "I do not agree with the contents of that ad."
Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was "a Highly Respected Democrat" and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is "virtually unprecedented."

"Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did," Trump wrote. "It's a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!"
